subject: English
topic: Grammar Usage — Active/Passive, Reported Speech, Conditionals, Modals and Subjunctive (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Change to passive voice: 'The committee will announce the results tomorrow.'

options.option_text: The results will be announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results will have been announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results shall be announced by the committee tomorrow.
The results are announced by the committee tomorrow.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Active: 'will announce' (future simple active). Passive: 'will be + past participle' → 'will be announced'. Structure: Object (The results) + will be + past participle (announced) + by + Subject (the committee) + time (tomorrow). Trap: 'will have been announced' = future perfect passive (wrong tense — used for future perfect active 'will have announced', not simple future); 'shall be announced' = 'shall' is for first person (I/We), not third person (the committee); present tense passive = wrong tense.

questions.stem: Change to active voice: 'The letter was being written by her when I arrived.'

options.option_text: She has written the letter when I arrived.
She was writing the letter when I arrived.
She wrote the letter when I arrived.
She had written the letter when I arrived.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Passive: 'was being written' = past continuous passive. Active equivalent: 'was + verb-ing' = past continuous active = 'was writing'. The continuous aspect ('being written') shows an ongoing action interrupted by my arrival. 'She was writing the letter when I arrived' ✓. Trap: 'wrote' = past simple (drops the continuous aspect — implies completion, but 'was being written' implies an action in progress); 'has written' = present perfect (wrong tense).

questions.stem: Convert to reported speech: She said, 'I am preparing for the exam now.'

options.option_text: She said that she is preparing for the exam then.
She said that she was preparing for the exam then.
She said that she had prepared for the exam now.
She said that she would prepare for the exam then.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Rules for reported speech (past reporting verb 'said'): (1) Present continuous → Past continuous: 'am preparing' → 'was preparing'. (2) 'now' → 'then'. (3) First person 'I' → third person 'she'. Result: 'She said that she was preparing for the exam then.' Trap: 'is preparing' = keeps present tense (wrong — must backshift when reporting verb is past); 'had prepared' = past perfect (past perfect is used for simple past in direct speech: 'I prepared' → 'she had prepared'; here the original is continuous, not simple past).

questions.stem: Convert to reported speech: He asked me, 'Have you submitted your application?'

options.option_text: He asked me if I had submitted my application.
He asked me if I have submitted my application.
He asked me have I submitted my application.
He asked me that had I submitted my application.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Rules: (1) Yes/No question → use 'if/whether'. (2) Backshift: present perfect 'have submitted' → past perfect 'had submitted'. (3) 'you' → 'I' (perspective shift). (4) Remove question word order: 'Have you' → 'I had'. Result: 'He asked me IF I HAD SUBMITTED my application' ✓. Trap: 'have submitted' = no backshift (wrong when reporting verb is past); 'have I submitted' = keeps question inversion (wrong in reported speech — must use statement word order); 'that had I' = 'that' is used for statements, 'if/whether' for yes/no questions.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the TYPE 2 CONDITIONAL?

options.option_text: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
If I had known earlier, I would have informed you.
If I were the principal, I would change the dress code.
If she had worked harder, she would have passed.

questions.explanation: C is correct. TYPE 2 CONDITIONAL = hypothetical/unreal present situation: 'If + past tense + would/could + base verb'. 'If I WERE the principal' (note: 'were' used for all subjects in subjunctive Type 2 — not 'was'), 'I WOULD CHANGE...' ✓ = imagining yourself in a position you are not in. Trap: A = Type 1 (real/possible future: 'if + present simple + will'); B and D = Type 3 (unreal past: 'if + past perfect + would have + past participle'). Type 2 is for unreal PRESENT; Type 3 is for unreal PAST.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses MUST correctly in the sense of CERTAINTY (deduction), not obligation?

options.option_text: You must submit your form by Friday.
Students must wear uniforms in school.
She must be tired; she has been working since dawn.
We must leave before the storm arrives.

questions.explanation: C is correct. MUST has two main uses: (1) OBLIGATION ('You must submit...', 'must wear', 'must leave') = a rule or requirement; (2) LOGICAL CERTAINTY/DEDUCTION ('She must be tired' = I'm confident she is tired, based on the evidence of working since dawn). C uses 'must' for DEDUCTION based on evidence — a logical inference. Trap: A, B, D = all use 'must' for obligation (rules and requirements). The deduction use is identifiable by the presence of evidence in the context: 'she has been working since dawn' = evidence → 'must be tired' = deduction.

questions.stem: Choose the correct question tag: 'He hardly goes out, ___?'

options.option_text: does he
doesn't he
is he
isn't he

questions.explanation: A is correct. HARDLY is a negative adverb ('hardly goes' = almost never goes = a negative meaning). RULE: When the main clause contains a negative word (hardly, scarcely, never, seldom, rarely, no, nobody), the question tag must be POSITIVE. 'He hardly goes out' → tag = 'DOES he?' (positive tag). 'Hardly goes' = present simple → auxiliary 'does'. Trap: 'doesn't he' = DOUBLE NEGATIVE: 'hardly' (negative) + 'doesn't' (negative) = two negatives together = wrong. The tag after negative adverbs is always positive.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the GERUND correctly where an infinitive would be WRONG?

options.option_text: She hopes playing for the national team one day.
She decided quitting her job immediately.
She is looking forward to meeting the director.
She wants playing tennis every morning.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'LOOK FORWARD TO + gerund (-ing)' is a fixed phrase where 'to' is a PREPOSITION, not part of the infinitive. Therefore: 'looking forward to MEETING' (gerund) ✓. NOT 'looking forward to MEET' (infinitive). Trap: A: 'hope' takes INFINITIVE not gerund → 'hopes TO PLAY'; B: 'decide' takes INFINITIVE → 'decided TO QUIT'; D: 'want' takes INFINITIVE → 'wants TO PLAY'. Key: when 'to' is a preposition (look forward TO, object TO, in addition TO, accustomed TO), use GERUND, not infinitive.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses the SUBJUNCTIVE mood?

options.option_text: The doctor suggested that he rests for a week.
The doctor suggested that he rest for a week.
The doctor suggested that he should rests for a week.
The doctor suggested that he rested for a week.

questions.explanation: B is correct. SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD: Used after verbs of recommendation, suggestion, demand, insistence etc. (suggest, recommend, demand, insist, propose, order, request). Structure: that + subject + BASE FORM of verb (no -s, no -ed, no auxiliary). 'Suggested that he REST' (base form, no 's') ✓. Trap: 'rests' = adds -s for third person (wrong in subjunctive — no -s in base form); 'rested' = past tense (wrong in mandative subjunctive); 'should rests' = 'should + bare infinitive' is acceptable (alternative to subjunctive) but 'should rests' has the wrong verb form (must be 'should rest').

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an ABSOLUTE PHRASE (a phrase not grammatically connected to the main clause)?

options.option_text: Running down the stairs, he tripped and fell.
Her work completed, she left the office.
After finishing his meal, he went for a walk.
To complete the project, she worked through the night.

questions.explanation: B is correct. An ABSOLUTE PHRASE = a phrase that modifies the entire sentence but has its own SUBJECT (different from the main clause subject). B: 'Her work completed' — subject of this phrase is 'her work' (different from main clause subject 'she'). Absolute phrase structure: noun/pronoun + past participle (or present participle). 'Her work completed, she left' = once her work was completed, she left. Trap: A = 'Running down the stairs' = participial phrase (subject = 'he', same as main clause = NOT absolute); C = 'After finishing' = subordinate clause/participial phrase, not absolute; D = 'To complete' = infinitive phrase, not absolute.
